opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think my views have shifted quite a bit here, and I'd say mostly in the direction of being more skeptical than I used to be.

A few years ago, there was a line of thinking, and I was sympathetic to it, that went something like: the incentives of a normal for-profit company are going to push hard toward racing, cutting corners, and maximizing shareholder value. So if you can set up a company with an unusual structure, like a nonprofit board that controls a for-profit entity, or a capped-profit arrangement, or a long-term benefit trust, then maybe you can create an actor at the frontier that has the commercial engine to stay competitive but whose ultimate decision-makers are accountable to a mission rather than to profit. That seemed like a pretty elegant idea.

What I've come to appreciate is that these structures are a lot weaker in practice than they look on paper. When there's enormous money at stake, and enormous talent, and investors and employees whose wealth depends on the company continuing to do well, the formal governance documents are only one source of power among many. If a board tries to exercise its authority in a way that the people actually running the company, the employees, and the key partners don't accept, it can turn out that the board's power was more theoretical than real. We've seen some fairly public illustrations of that.

There's also a subtler issue, which is that even when nothing dramatic happens, the people sitting in these governance roles often don't have the information, the time, or the expertise to meaningfully second-guess a fast-moving frontier lab. So you can end up with something that provides a sense of reassurance without much actual constraint.

I don't think they're worthless. I think they can matter at the margin, they can shape culture, they can give some people inside the company a legitimate lever to pull, and they can create some friction against the worst decisions. But I've moved away from thinking of corporate governance innovation as one of the main ways we're going to get safety. I now put a lot more weight on things like external accountability: regulation, third-party evaluations and audits, transparency requirements, and on companies making specific, concrete commitments, like what they'll do if their models reach certain capability thresholds, that outsiders can actually check them against. Those feel more robust to me than hoping that the right board structure will hold up when it's really tested.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I'd say my view has gotten more pessimistic, or at least more humble, over the last few years.

Let me back up and say what I used to think. The idea was something like: the standard corporate form has a problem, which is that the people running the company have a fiduciary duty to shareholders, and shareholders mostly want profit. If you're building something that might be really dangerous for the world, you'd like the people in charge to have an obligation to the world, not just to the shareholders. So you set up something unusual. A nonprofit board that controls a for-profit subsidiary. A long-term benefit trust. A public benefit corporation. Some structure where there's a group of people whose job is explicitly to say "no" when the commercial incentives say "yes." And on paper, that looks like a pretty elegant solution. You're sort of baking the mission into the legal DNA of the company.

And I was involved in some of this, so I'm not coming at it as a neutral observer. I was on the OpenAI board for a while, and I've been close to a lot of the thinking behind these structures.

What I've come to appreciate is that a governance structure is only as strong as the willingness of everyone involved to actually respect it when it bites. And the moments when it bites are exactly the moments when there's enormous pressure not to respect it. If a board decides to do something unpopular, like remove a CEO, or slow down a product, or decline a huge investment, the question becomes: who actually has the power here? Is it the people with the legal authority on paper, or is it the people who control the employees, the compute, the investor relationships, the public narrative? And what we've seen, I think pretty clearly, is that the paper authority can turn out to be a lot weaker than it looks. Employees can walk. Investors can threaten. The media can turn. And the structure doesn't really have an enforcement mechanism against that. It just has words in a document.

So one update is: these structures are more fragile than I thought. They work fine as long as nobody really needs them to work, and then they get tested at exactly the wrong time.

A second update is about the people problem. Even if the structure holds, you need the people sitting in those seats to have the information, the expertise, the time, and the independence to actually make good calls. And that's really hard. Board members are usually part-time. They're hearing about things from management. They often don't have the technical depth to evaluate what they're being told. And the pool of people who are both deeply knowledgeable about frontier AI and genuinely independent of the companies is tiny, because the companies are where the knowledge is. So you end up with boards that are either independent but under-informed, or well-informed but entangled.

The third thing, and this is maybe the one I'd emphasize most, is that I've moved toward thinking that whatever these structures do, they're a complement to external accountability, not a substitute for it. I used to think of them as kind of a first line of defense. Now I think of them more as a nice-to-have. The things that actually constrain companies in a durable way tend to come from outside: regulation, legal liability, industry standards that are verified by third parties, public and employee pressure, and honestly competition that makes safety a selling point. Self-governance, however cleverly designed, is a company promising to police itself, and the history of other industries is not encouraging on that.

Now, I don't want to swing all the way to saying they're useless. I still think they do a few real things. They create a venue where someone is supposed to be asking the hard questions, which is better than nobody asking. They can give cover to people inside the company who want to push back. They send a signal about what the company says it values, which is at least something you can hold them to later. And they can shape culture, which matters a lot in practice. I just think of all of that as a modest effect rather than a safeguard you'd want to bet civilization on.

If I had to summarize it, I'd say: I went from thinking of unusual governance structures as a potentially important lever to thinking of them as a weak and somewhat unreliable one, and I've shifted my attention correspondingly toward things like evaluations, transparency requirements, and the broader policy ecosystem. I'd rather have a world where companies are being watched and tested by people who don't work for them than a world where we're relying on the companies to have designed themselves well. Both would be nice. But if I could only have one, it's not close.

astra-6.text:
I think I’ve become more skeptical. There’s an appealing idea here: if the commercial incentives are going to push a company toward taking too much risk, you can give ultimate authority to a board whose job is to put the public interest first. And that could matter. I wouldn’t say governance structures are irrelevant.

But a formal right to make a decision is different from the practical ability to make it stick. You need people to cooperate with you. You need the information to know when to intervene. And you need to be able to withstand a situation where employees, investors, or partners strongly disagree with what you’re doing. A structure on paper doesn’t automatically give you any of those things.

There’s also the question of what you’re actually asking the board to do. “Make sure this goes well for humanity” is a very difficult mandate to act on. It’s much more useful if there are concrete commitments, clear procedures for assessing risk, and some shared understanding of what would justify slowing down.

So I’d put less weight on an unusual governance structure as a solution in itself, and more weight on whether the organization has credible, operational ways to make and enforce safety decisions. The structure can support those things, but it can’t substitute for them.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become more skeptical. I still think governance matters, but I’m less optimistic that you can write down an unusual structure and have it reliably produce good decisions when the stakes get very high.

There’s a tempting picture where you say, “The company has a board whose duty is to humanity, rather than to shareholders, so if there’s a conflict between safety and profit, safety wins.” But that leaves a lot unanswered. Does the board have the information it needs? Can it tell whether management is making a reasonable judgment? And if it makes a decision that employees and investors strongly oppose, can it actually make that decision stick?

So I’d now put more weight on how power works in practice: who understands what’s happening, who has credibility, who can replace whom, and what happens when people disagree. The formal structure is one part of that, but it’s not a substitute for it.

I haven’t concluded that unusual governance structures are useless. I think they can create room for people to do the right thing. I’m just much less inclined to treat the existence of one as strong evidence that a company will handle a really difficult safety decision well.
